chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Ahmad ibn Asheym, from one of our companions who said:

One of our family members had fever, so the physicians prescribed Al-Ghafis (a herb) for him. So we made him drink it, but he did not benefit from it. So I complained of that to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him), so he (peace be upon him) said: 'Allah has not Made a healing in anything from the bitter. Take a (lump of) sugar and a half, so grind it in a vessel and pour water over it until it melts in it, and place iron over it, and apportion it from the beginning of the night. So when it becomes (a solution), so take it with your hand and make him drink it. So when it is the second night, so make it with two (lumps of) sugar and a half, and apportion it just as you had done beforehand, and make him drink it. And when it was the third night, so take three (lumps of) sugar and a half, and apportion it like that'. He (the narrator) said, 'So I did, and Allah Mighty and Majestic Healed our sick'.

key_terms.الْغَافِث: A specific herb used for medicinal purposes
key_terms.سُكَّرَة: A lump or piece of sugar
key_terms.نَجْمُهَا: To let it steep or sit (referring to the preparation process)

ai.seo_question: What is the prophetic medical remedy for fever involving sugar and iron mentioned in Al-Kafi?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) corrects the prevailing medical assumption that bitterness is always therapeutic, prescribing instead a sweet remedy of sugar and water infused with iron (*al-hadid*) over three nights. This narrative highlights the Shia scholarly tradition of integrating practical pharmacology with spiritual trust, demonstrating the Imam’s authority in diagnosing the specific nature of the ailment beyond conventional wisdom. The gradual increase in dosage reflects a methodical approach to treatment, emphasizing both empirical observation and divine healing (*shifa*).
